lessons.title: Context: Victorian Empire & Crime
lessons.description: Victorian Empire, crime fiction, opium and cocaine, and Doyle’s world in The Sign of Four.
lessons.content_html:
The World Doyle Wrote For

Arthur Conan Doyle published The Sign of Four in 1890, during the height of the Victorian era. Britain ruled the largest empire the world had ever seen, stretching across India, Africa and the Caribbean. The novel is soaked in the consequences of that empire: the Agra treasure comes from India, Jonathan Small lost his leg serving in the Indian army, and Tonga is brought to England from the Andaman Islands. For a Victorian reader, the empire was a source of national pride — but Doyle shows its darker side, where colonial violence follows people home.

Understanding this context is essential For the exam . The examiners test your ability to connect Doyle’s choices to the world he was writing in, using AO3 (context). Every reference to India, the army, and the treasure links back to the realities of empire.

Key Fact

The British Empire is central to the plot. The Agra treasure was stolen during the Indian Rebellion of 1857, Jonathan Small served as a soldier in India, and Tonga comes from the colonised Andaman Islands. Doyle shows that imperial violence abroad creates consequences at home in London.

Victorian London: Fog, Poverty and Class

The London of The Sign of Four is a city of extremes. Doyle moves his characters between wealthy drawing rooms and the grimy docks of the Thames, between the respectable homes of Camberwell and the opium den in Upper Swandam Lane. This contrast reflects the stark class divide of Victorian society. Mary Morstan is a governess — educated but without money. Thaddeus Sholto lives in gaudy luxury. The dockworkers and street children (the Baker Street Irregulars) represent London’s poorest.

Doyle uses London’s fog and darkness as more than setting. The fog represents moral confusion and hidden truths. Watson describes a “dense drizzly fog” that hangs over the city as they travel to Pondicherry Lodge — they literally cannot see what lies ahead, just as they cannot yet see the solution to the mystery.

The novel opens with Holmes injecting a “seven-per-cent solution” of cocaine. In 1890, this was perfectly legal. Cocaine and opium were widely available in pharmacies and were even found in everyday products. However, attitudes were beginning to shift, and Watson’s disapproval in Chapter 1 reflects growing medical concern. Doyle, himself a trained doctor, uses Holmes’s drug use to show that his brilliant mind becomes self-destructive without intellectual stimulation. The drugs are not glamorised — Watson calls the habit a “pathological and morbid process.”

The opium trade was also tied to empire. Britain had fought two Opium Wars with China (1839–1842 and 1856–1860) to protect its hugely profitable trade in the drug. The presence of opium in the novel is another thread connecting London back to imperial exploitation.

The Rise of Detective Fiction

Doyle was not the first writer of detective fiction, but he made it massively popular. Edgar Allan Poe’s C. Auguste Dupin stories (from the 1840s) and Wilkie Collins’s The Moonstone (1868) established the genre. However, Doyle created the template that still dominates today: a genius detective with a loyal companion who narrates the story. Holmes uses deductive reasoning — observing tiny physical details and drawing logical conclusions — which reflected the Victorian fascination with science and rational thought.

The 1880s also saw the creation of the Metropolitan Police’s Criminal Investigation Department (CID). Real detectives were becoming public figures, and Doyle tapped into this cultural moment. Holmes’s superiority over the police detective Athelney Jones reflects a popular Victorian view that official institutions were often slow and incompetent compared to brilliant individuals.

Key Fact

Doyle built on earlier detective fiction by Poe (C. Auguste Dupin) and Collins (The Moonstone), but created the definitive template: a genius detective using scientific deduction, narrated by a loyal but less brilliant companion. This pairing of Holmes and Watson influenced virtually all detective fiction that followed.

Doyle (1859–1930) was born in Edinburgh and trained as a doctor at the University of Edinburgh. His medical professor, Dr Joseph Bell, was famous for diagnosing patients through close observation of tiny physical details — the direct inspiration for Sherlock Holmes. Doyle struggled to attract patients to his medical practice, so he began writing fiction to supplement his income. A Study in Scarlet (1887) introduced Holmes, and The Sign of Four (1890) was the second Holmes novel, commissioned by Lippincott’s Magazine at a dinner where Oscar Wilde was also present.

Doyle’s medical training is visible throughout the novel. Watson is a doctor and army veteran; Holmes approaches crime like a scientist examining evidence in a laboratory. The emphasis on observation, evidence and logic reflects the Victorian belief in empiricism — that truth could be discovered through careful study of the physical world.

Why This Context Matters in the Exam

AQA Paper 1, Section B gives you an extract from The Sign of Four and asks you to write about the extract and the novel as a whole. AO3 (context) runs through the entire question — you must show understanding of how Doyle’s choices connect to Victorian society, empire, class, gender, science and the detective genre. The strongest responses weave context into every paragraph rather than adding it as a separate block.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the AQA Paper 1 Section B question on The Sign of Four, you are given an extract and must write about both the extract and the novel as a whole. Context (AO3) should be embedded within your analysis, not bolted on. Instead of writing “Victorians were interested in the empire,” link it to a specific moment: “Doyle’s choice to set the treasure’s origins in colonial India reflects Victorian anxieties about the moral cost of empire.” Always connect context to a quotation or technique.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The British Empire is central to the plot — the Agra treasure, Jonathan Small’s service in India, and Tonga’s origins all connect to colonial exploitation.
  • Holmes’s cocaine use reflects both Victorian drug culture and Doyle’s theme that a brilliant mind without stimulation becomes self-destructive.
  • Doyle created the definitive detective fiction template, drawing on his medical training, Poe’s Dupin stories, and the Victorian faith in science and rational thought.

practice_questions.text: Read the opening of Chapter 1, from ‘Sherlock Holmes took his bottle from the corner of the mantelpiece’ to ‘a seven-per-cent solution.’ How does Doyle use language in this extract to introduce Holmes’s character?

Watson’s observation establishes the narrative perspective — the reader sees Holmes through a concerned friend’s eyes. The casual ritual of the injection suggests habitual use, normalising something that Watson finds alarming. Context: cocaine was legal in 1890, but Doyle (a trained doctor) uses Watson’s disapproval to signal growing medical concern.

lessons.title: Chapters 1-4: The Mystery Begins
lessons.description: Holmes’s cocaine habit, Mary Morstan’s mystery, Thaddeus Sholto and the horror at Pondicherry Lodge.
lessons.content_html:
Chapter 1: Holmes, Watson and Cocaine

The novel opens not with a crime, but with a character study. Sherlock Holmes reaches for his hypodermic syringe and injects a “seven-per-cent solution” of cocaine. Watson watches with open disapproval, calling it a “pathological and morbid process.” This opening immediately establishes two things: Holmes’s extraordinary mind needs constant stimulation, and Watson serves as both narrator and moral conscience.

Holmes explains: “My mind rebels at stagnation. Give me problems, give me work.” Without a case, his brilliance turns inward and becomes destructive. Doyle uses this opening to show that Holmes is not a conventional hero — he is flawed, restless and potentially self-destructive. The cocaine is not glamorised; Watson’s medical perspective ensures the reader understands the danger.

Key Fact

Holmes tells Watson: “My mind rebels at stagnation.” He uses cocaine to escape boredom when no case occupies his intellect. Watson, as a doctor, calls it a “pathological and morbid process” — Doyle uses Watson’s disapproval to show the habit is harmful, not heroic.

Holmes also demonstrates his deductive method by analysing Watson’s pocket watch. From scratches, dents and a pawnbroker’s mark, Holmes deduces that Watson’s late brother was an alcoholic who squandered his inheritance. Watson is hurt and angry, revealing tension beneath their friendship. This scene establishes that Holmes’s deductions, while brilliant, can be cold and invasive.

Chapter 2: Mary Morstan’s Case

Governess Mary Morstan arrives at Baker Street with a compelling mystery. Her father, Captain Arthur Morstan, vanished ten years ago after returning from India. Since then, she has received an anonymous pearl every year, and now an unsigned letter invites her to a meeting. Holmes is immediately energised — he has a problem to solve.

Mary is presented as composed, brave and practical. Watson is immediately attracted to her, noting her “sweet and amiable” expression. Doyle uses Watson’s romantic interest to create a secondary plot thread alongside the mystery. Importantly, Watson notes that if the treasure is found, Mary will be wealthy — and as a man of modest means, he feels he cannot honourably declare his feelings to a rich woman. This reflects Victorian attitudes to courtship and class.

The trio travel through foggy London to meet Thaddeus Sholto, one of the sons of Major John Sholto. Thaddeus is a memorable comic creation — nervous, theatrical, obsessed with his own health, and surrounded by Eastern art and luxury. He reveals the backstory: his father, Major Sholto, had been Captain Morstan’s fellow officer in India. They both knew of the Agra treasure. Major Sholto stole the treasure for himself, and Captain Morstan died of a heart attack during an argument about it.

Thaddeus has been secretly sending Mary the pearls out of guilt. He explains that his twin brother, Bartholomew, has now found the treasure hidden in the attic of their family home, Pondicherry Lodge. He invites them to claim Mary’s share.

Chapter 4: The Horror at Pondicherry Lodge

When they arrive at Pondicherry Lodge, the housekeeper is frantic — Bartholomew Sholto’s room is locked from inside. Holmes and Watson break in to find Bartholomew dead, his face frozen in a terrible grin. A poison dart is embedded in his scalp, and the treasure chest is empty. On the table is a card reading “The sign of the four.”

This is the novel’s most Gothic moment. Doyle uses horror conventions — the locked room, the distorted corpse, the mysterious calling card — to heighten tension. The locked-room mystery was a popular device in detective fiction, creating an apparently impossible crime that only Holmes’s logic can solve. Watson describes Bartholomew’s face as wearing a “horrible smile, a fixed and unnatural grin” — the poison causes involuntary muscle contraction, but the effect is deeply unsettling.

Key Fact

At Pondicherry Lodge, Holmes finds three crucial clues: a small footprint (Tonga), the marks of a wooden leg (Jonathan Small), and creosote on the rope used to enter through the roof. The card reading “The sign of the four” connects the murder to the original pact over the Agra treasure in India.

The locked-room mystery was a staple of Victorian detective fiction. Poe used it in ‘The Murders in the Rue Morgue’ (1841). In The Sign of Four, Bartholomew’s room is bolted from inside, yet someone has entered, murdered him, and stolen the treasure. Holmes solves it by looking upward — the killer entered through a trapdoor in the roof. This demonstrates Holmes’s ability to see what others miss, and Doyle’s skill in using genre conventions to create suspense while ultimately providing a rational explanation.

How Doyle Builds Suspense in Chapters 1–4

Doyle structures these opening chapters as a crescendo. Chapter 1 is slow and domestic — two friends in a sitting room. Chapter 2 introduces the mystery. Chapter 3 raises the stakes with Thaddeus’s revelation. Chapter 4 delivers the shock of murder. Each chapter increases the tension, drawing the reader deeper into the plot. Watson’s first-person narration limits what the reader knows, creating suspense because we discover clues at the same pace as Watson — always one step behind Holmes.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about Chapters 1–4 in the exam, focus on how Doyle establishes character through action and dialogue rather than description. Holmes is characterised by what he does (injecting cocaine, analysing the watch) more than what he says about himself. Similarly, the setting of foggy London is not just atmosphere — it reflects the mystery’s moral confusion. Always link technique to effect on the reader.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The opening chapter establishes Holmes as a flawed genius whose brilliant mind becomes self-destructive without intellectual stimulation — his cocaine use is a character study, not just a plot detail.
  • Mary Morstan’s arrival provides both the mystery (her father’s disappearance, the pearls) and a romantic subplot that reflects Victorian class anxieties.
  • Bartholomew Sholto’s murder at Pondicherry Lodge uses Gothic horror and the locked-room mystery convention to create the novel’s central crime scene.

lessons.title: Chapters 5-8: The Chase
lessons.description: The crime scene clues, Toby the dog, Holmes’s deductions and the Baker Street Irregulars.
lessons.content_html:
Chapter 5: Holmes at the Crime Scene

While Athelney Jones of Scotland Yard arrests the wrong man (Thaddeus Sholto), Holmes conducts his own methodical investigation. He examines the rooftop, finds footprints and measures them with a tape. He identifies two intruders: one with a wooden leg and one with bare, unusually small feet. He discovers creosote on the rope used to climb into the attic. Every observation reflects the deductive approach he will articulate explicitly in Chapter 6: “when you have eliminated the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth.” (Note: this famous line is from Chapter 6, not Chapter 5)

Doyle contrasts Holmes’s careful, scientific approach with Jones’s blundering. Jones immediately suspects Thaddeus because he was at the scene and had a motive — a classic mistake of jumping to conclusions based on circumstantial evidence. Holmes, by contrast, follows the physical evidence. This contrast reinforces the novel’s central message about the superiority of scientific detection over conventional police work.

Key Fact

“When you have eliminated the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth.” This is Holmes’s most famous principle of deduction. At Pondicherry Lodge, he applies it systematically: the room was locked, so entry must have been from above; the small footprint and wooden-leg mark identify two distinct intruders; the creosote provides a scent trail.

Chapter 6: Toby the Dog

Holmes borrows Toby, a half-spaniel, half-lurcher with an extraordinary sense of smell, from his friend Mr Sherman. Using the creosote from the crime scene, Holmes sets Toby on the trail of the killers. The dog leads them on a long chase through south London — past factories, timber yards and working-class streets — before arriving at a barrel of creosote in a yard. The trail has led to a dead end. Toby has followed the strongest creosote scent, not the killers’ trail.

This false trail is structurally important. Doyle uses it to slow the pace, create a setback, and remind the reader that detection is not always straightforward. Holmes responds with characteristic good humour: “I have been at some small expense over this matter, which I shall expect the county to refund.” Even when wrong, Holmes is unflappable. Toby is then set on the correct trail, which leads them towards the river.

Throughout Chapters 5–7, Doyle showcases Holmes’s method in extraordinary detail. At Pondicherry Lodge, Holmes deduces that the smaller intruder is from “one of the Indian islands” based on the shape and size of the footprint, and that he uses a poisoned dart — a weapon associated with indigenous peoples of the Andaman Islands. From the wooden-leg marks, Holmes knows the other intruder is Jonathan Small.

Holmes’s method follows a clear pattern: observe physical evidence, eliminate impossibilities, form a hypothesis, then test it. This mirrors the scientific method that Victorians revered. Doyle, trained as a doctor, essentially transplants medical diagnosis into criminal investigation.

Chapter 7: The Baker Street Irregulars

When Toby’s trail reaches the river, Holmes deploys the Baker Street Irregulars — a gang of street children led by a boy called Wiggins. Holmes pays them a shilling each to search every boatyard along the Thames for a steam launch called the Aurora. The Irregulars can “go everywhere, see everything, overhear every one” without attracting suspicion, because Victorian society largely ignored poor children.

Doyle’s use of the Irregulars serves several purposes. Practically, they extend Holmes’s reach across London. Socially, they reveal the poverty of Victorian street children — they are eager to work for a shilling because they have nothing. Thematically, they show Holmes operating outside official structures. While Athelney Jones works through bureaucracy, Holmes uses an informal network of the city’s poorest inhabitants. This reflects a Victorian tension between official institutions and individual enterprise.

Key Fact

Holmes uses three investigative tools: his own deductive reasoning (physical evidence at the crime scene), Toby the dog (tracking the creosote scent), and the Baker Street Irregulars (searching the Thames boatyards). Each represents a different approach — science, instinct and street knowledge — and all operate outside the official police investigation.

Chapter 8: Athelney Jones — The Official Detective

Athelney Jones is Doyle’s comic foil to Holmes. Jones is confident, loud and wrong. He arrests Thaddeus Sholto based on circumstantial evidence and announces his theory with total certainty, only to be forced to release him when the evidence collapses. Jones embodies everything Holmes criticises about conventional detection: theory before evidence, assumptions before observation.

Holmes warns: “It is a capital mistake to theorise before you have all the evidence. It biases the judgment.” Jones does exactly this — he forms a theory (Thaddeus is guilty) and then looks for evidence to support it. Holmes does the opposite: he gathers evidence first and lets it lead to a conclusion. This contrast reflects a broader Victorian debate about the proper role of science in society. The new Metropolitan Police CID (founded 1878) was still finding its methods, and Doyle’s fiction championed a more rigorous, evidence-based approach.

Despite his failures, Jones is not entirely unsympathetic. He eventually comes to Holmes for help, showing humility. By the end of the novel, Jones takes credit for the capture, but Holmes does not mind — he cares about solving the puzzle, not public recognition.

These chapters establish the novel’s central tension between two ways of understanding the world: rational, evidence-based deduction versus assumption and prejudice. Holmes represents the Enlightenment ideal of reason; Jones represents institutional complacency. For a Victorian readership that valued progress and science, Holmes was the aspirational figure.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When analysing Holmes’s deductive method in the exam, always connect his techniques to the wider theme of science versus assumption. Don’t just describe what Holmes does — explain why Doyle presents it this way. The contrast between Holmes and Athelney Jones is a gift for AO2 (methods): Doyle uses the foil character to highlight Holmes’s superiority and champion the Victorian ideal of rational inquiry.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Holmes’s principle — “eliminate the impossible” — drives the investigation: physical evidence at the crime scene identifies the wooden-legged man and the small-footed killer.
  • Toby’s false trail and the Baker Street Irregulars show that detection involves setbacks and unconventional methods, not just individual genius.
  • The contrast between Holmes (evidence-first) and Athelney Jones (theory-first) embodies the Victorian tension between scientific reasoning and institutional assumption.

lessons.title: Chapters 9-12: The Resolution
lessons.description: The Thames chase, Small’s confession, the lost treasure and Holmes’s return to cocaine.
lessons.content_html:
Chapter 9: The Thames Chase

The Thames chase is the novel’s most dramatic set piece. Holmes hires a police launch and, with Watson and Athelney Jones aboard, pursues Jonathan Small and Tonga down the river at night. Doyle fills the scene with vivid sensory detail: the dark water, the throbbing engines, the distant lights of London’s docklands. Watson describes “the barges and the riverside buildings racing past us” as the boats cut through the water at high speed.

The chase serves multiple purposes. It provides thrilling action after the intellectual puzzle of the earlier chapters. It moves the story from the drawing rooms of Upper Norwood to the industrial Thames — from the respectable face of Victorian London to its working waterfront. And it ends in violence: Tonga fires a blowpipe dart at the pursuers, narrowly missing Watson. Holmes and Watson fire back, and Tonga is shot and falls into the river, where his body is never recovered.

Key Fact

During the chase, Tonga fires a poison dart at the police launch. Holmes and Watson return fire, and Tonga falls dead into the Thames. Jonathan Small, realising he cannot escape, throws the Agra treasure overboard piece by piece into the river. The treasure that drove the entire plot is lost forever.

Tonga’s Death and Victorian Racial Attitudes

Tonga’s death is troubling from a modern perspective. He is shot without hesitation and his body sinks unrecovered into the Thames — no character mourns him. Doyle describes Tonga using language that reflects deeply racist Victorian attitudes: he is called a “savage,” “unhallowed dwarf,” and compared to an animal. Holmes earlier deduced his origins from a colonial gazetteer that describes the Andaman Islanders as “naturally hideous” and “fierce, morose, and intractable.”

In the exam, you should acknowledge that Doyle’s portrayal of Tonga reflects the racial prejudice of his era. Victorian Britain widely believed in a racial hierarchy that placed white Europeans at the top. Tonga is not given a voice, a backstory, or any humanity — he exists in the novel only as a weapon and a threat. Jonathan Small, by contrast, is given a full confession and the chance to explain himself. This disparity reveals whose stories Victorian society valued and whose it erased.

Chapters 11 and 12 are Jonathan Small’s extended confession, narrated in his own voice. Small was a young British soldier serving in India when he lost his leg to a crocodile. During the Indian Rebellion of 1857, he was posted to guard the Agra fort. A Sikh servant named Abdullah Khan offered Small a share of a vast treasure in exchange for his help in ambushing a merchant. Small agreed. They murdered the merchant and swore a pact — the “sign of the four” — with three Sikh companions, each signing with their names.

Small was caught and imprisoned in the Andaman Islands, where he befriended Tonga. He revealed the treasure’s location to Major Sholto and Captain Morstan in exchange for help escaping, but Sholto betrayed him and took the treasure. Small spent years plotting revenge. His confession is sympathetic in places — he feels genuinely wronged by Sholto — but he also participated in murder and shows no remorse for the merchant’s death.

The Agra Treasure: Greed and Its Consequences

The Agra treasure is the engine of the entire plot. Every crime in the novel flows from it: the original murder of the merchant, Small’s imprisonment, Sholto’s betrayal, Morstan’s death, Bartholomew’s murder, and the Thames chase. Yet the treasure itself is ultimately worthless — Small throws it into the river rather than let anyone else have it. “I would rather that our old cronies at Doolan had it than that a soul of us should benefit from it,” he says.

Doyle uses the treasure to explore the theme of greed. Everyone who touches the treasure suffers: the original merchant is murdered, the four conspirators are imprisoned, Sholto dies tormented by guilt, Morstan dies in an argument over it, Bartholomew is murdered for it, and Small loses both the treasure and his freedom. The moral is clear: the treasure brings nothing but suffering.

Key Fact

The Agra treasure destroys everyone who pursues it. The merchant is murdered for it, the four conspirators are imprisoned, Sholto and Morstan both die because of it, Bartholomew is killed, and Small throws it into the Thames. Doyle’s message is that greed corrupts and that stolen wealth brings only suffering.

Chapter 12: The Ending — Love and Cocaine

With the treasure lost, Watson realises Mary Morstan will remain poor — which removes the class barrier to their relationship. He proposes and she accepts. Watson’s joy contrasts sharply with Holmes’s reaction. Holmes shows no interest in the romance and, with the case solved, returns immediately to his cocaine. The novel ends as it began: Holmes reaching for the syringe.

The novel’s cyclical structure is significant. It opens with cocaine and closes with cocaine, suggesting that Holmes’s restlessness cannot be permanently satisfied. Each case is only a temporary reprieve. The structure also contrasts Holmes and Watson: Watson moves forward (marriage, emotional fulfilment) while Holmes remains trapped in a cycle (case, cocaine, case). This ending raises questions about whether Holmes’s genius is a gift or a burden.

The contrast between the two endings — Watson’s romantic happiness and Holmes’s solitary cocaine use — mirrors the novel’s dual structure throughout. Watson represents emotion, warmth and human connection; Holmes represents intellect, isolation and obsessive focus. Doyle suggests that neither approach alone is complete.

The resolution of The Sign of Four is deliberately bittersweet. Justice is served (Small is captured), the mystery is solved, and Watson finds love. But the treasure is lost, Tonga is dead, Holmes is back on cocaine, and the underlying causes — imperial greed, social inequality — remain unchanged. Doyle does not offer a neat, triumphant ending.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The ending of The Sign of Four is rich territory for essay questions. If asked about structure, discuss the cyclical pattern (cocaine to cocaine). If asked about character, contrast Watson’s emotional growth with Holmes’s stasis. If asked about themes, explore how the lost treasure symbolises the futility of greed. Always connect your analysis to Doyle’s methods (AO2) and Victorian context (AO3).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Thames chase is the novel’s dramatic climax — Tonga is killed, Small is captured, and the treasure is thrown into the river, making the object everyone fought over worthless.
  • Jonathan Small’s confession reveals the full history of the Agra treasure, connecting every crime in the novel back to imperial India and the original act of greed.
  • The cyclical structure (cocaine to cocaine) suggests Holmes’s brilliance is both a gift and a curse, and contrasts with Watson’s emotional fulfilment through marriage to Mary.

lessons.title: Character Analysis
lessons.description: Holmes, Watson, Mary Morstan, Jonathan Small, Tonga and Thaddeus Sholto analysed in depth.
lessons.content_html:
Sherlock Holmes: The Flawed Genius

Holmes is not a conventional hero. He is brilliant, arrogant, emotionally detached, and addicted to cocaine. Doyle presents him as a man whose extraordinary intellect is both his greatest strength and his deepest flaw. When he has a case, Holmes is electric: focused, energetic, capable of astonishing deductions. Without a case, he collapses into boredom and self-destruction. His opening line about his mind rebelling “at stagnation” defines his entire character arc.

Holmes’s deductive method is his defining quality. He reads Watson’s watch like a scientist reads data. At Pondicherry Lodge, he measures footprints, identifies creosote, and reconstructs the crime while Jones blunders. His famous maxim — “eliminate the impossible” — encapsulates the Victorian ideal of rational inquiry. Yet his rationality has limits: he cannot sustain emotional relationships, he dismisses Watson’s romantic feelings, and he returns to cocaine the moment the intellectual challenge ends.

Key Fact

Holmes is characterised by three tensions: intellectual brilliance (“eliminate the impossible”), emotional detachment (he dismisses Watson’s engagement with the cocaine syringe), and self-destructive restlessness (“my mind rebels at stagnation”). For the exam, always analyse Holmes through these contrasts rather than treating him as simply ‘clever.’

Dr John Watson: Narrator and Moral Centre

Watson is far more than Holmes’s sidekick. As the first-person narrator, he controls everything the reader sees. He is honest, warm, brave, and morally grounded — qualities that contrast with Holmes’s cold brilliance. Watson served in Afghanistan and was wounded by a Jezail bullet (as established in A Study in Scarlet; The Sign of Four only mentions a old wound without naming the Battle of Maiwand specifically); he embodies Victorian ideals of duty, honour and masculine stoicism.

Watson’s role as narrator is crucial for the mystery genre. Because Watson is intelligent but not as brilliant as Holmes, the reader discovers clues at Watson’s pace — always one step behind Holmes. This creates suspense. Watson’s romantic subplot with Mary Morstan adds emotional depth. His awareness that the treasure would make Mary rich and therefore ‘above’ him reveals the class anxieties of Victorian courtship. When the treasure is lost, Watson is relieved rather than disappointed — he values love over wealth.

Mary Morstan challenges some Victorian gender expectations while conforming to others. She is brave: she comes to Baker Street alone, accompanies the men into danger at Pondicherry Lodge, and does not faint or become hysterical at the sight of Bartholomew’s body. Watson describes her as having “a sweet and amiable expression” but also “a firm set of her lips” — Doyle gives her both warmth and determination.

However, Mary is also defined by her relationship to men. Her story begins with her father’s disappearance and ends with Watson’s proposal. She is a governess — respectable but dependent. The treasure would have given her independence, but its loss is presented as a blessing because it allows Watson to propose. Doyle does not question whether Mary might have wanted the independence that wealth would bring. For the exam, you can analyse Mary as both stronger than the typical Victorian heroine and still constrained by the era’s gender norms.

Jonathan Small: Villain or Victim?

Jonathan Small is the novel’s most complex character. He is both the antagonist — responsible for Bartholomew’s murder and the chase — and a sympathetic villain. His confession in Chapters 11–12 reveals a man shaped by empire: he lost his leg serving in India, was drawn into the treasure plot by circumstance, and was then betrayed by Major Sholto. He has a genuine grievance.

However, Small is not innocent. He participated in the murder of the merchant without apparent remorse, and he brought Tonga to London knowing Tonga would kill. His throwing of the treasure into the Thames is an act of spite as much as principle. Doyle complicates the reader’s response: you can sympathise with Small’s sense of injustice while recognising his violence. This moral ambiguity is excellent exam material — it shows Doyle questioning simple categories of ‘hero’ and ‘villain.’

Key Fact

Small is both villain and victim. Villain: he murdered the merchant, he brought Tonga to kill Bartholomew, he destroyed the treasure out of spite. Victim: he lost his leg in imperial service, he was betrayed by Sholto, he spent decades imprisoned. Doyle deliberately complicates moral judgment — the exam rewards students who explore this ambiguity.

Tonga: The Silenced Character

Tonga is the novel’s most troubling figure. He is an Andaman Islander whom Small befriended in prison, and he is fiercely loyal — Small calls him “staunch and true.” Yet Doyle never gives Tonga a voice. He does not speak a single line of dialogue. He is described using dehumanising language drawn from colonial gazetteers: “savage,” “unhallowed dwarf,” “naturally hideous.” He kills Bartholomew with a blowpipe dart and is himself killed without mourning. In the exam, Tonga is essential for AO3: his treatment reveals the racial prejudice embedded in Victorian literature and colonial attitudes.

Thaddeus Sholto is one of Doyle’s most vivid comic creations. He is anxious, theatrical, a hypochondriac, and surrounded by expensive Eastern art. His nervousness provides comic contrast to the growing danger of the plot. Yet he also has a conscience: he has been sending Mary the pearls out of guilt for his father’s theft. Thaddeus represents the possibility of moral redemption within a corrupt family. His wrongful arrest by Jones adds dramatic irony — the most morally honest of the Sholtos is the one punished.

Thaddeus also functions as a foil to his twin brother Bartholomew. While Bartholomew hoards the treasure, Thaddeus wants to share it. Their different responses to inherited wealth show that individuals can choose differently even within the same circumstances.

In the exam, you will score highly by showing how characters function in relation to each other. Holmes and Watson are complementary opposites. Small and Sholto mirror each other as men corrupted by the treasure. Mary and Holmes represent emotion versus intellect. Tonga and the Irregulars are both marginalised figures used by more powerful characters. Character analysis in The Sign of Four is always about relationships, not individuals in isolation.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about character in the exam, avoid simply describing what a character does. Instead, analyse how Doyle presents them (AO2) and why (AO3). For Holmes, discuss the tension between genius and self-destruction. For Mary, explore how she both challenges and conforms to Victorian gender norms. For Small, argue whether he is a villain or a victim. The examiner rewards nuanced analysis, not plot retelling.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Holmes is a flawed genius — brilliant but emotionally detached and self-destructive. His deductive method reflects Victorian faith in science, but his cocaine habit shows the limits of pure intellect.
  • Jonathan Small is both villain and victim, and Tonga is the novel’s most silenced character — both are essential for exploring Doyle’s presentation of empire and racial prejudice.
  • Characters work best when analysed in relation to each other: Holmes/Watson, Small/Sholto, Mary/Holmes, Tonga/the Irregulars.

lessons.title: Setting, Structure & Detection
lessons.description: London as setting, dual narrative, clues and red herrings, and the science of deduction.
lessons.content_html:
Victorian London: More Than a Backdrop

London in The Sign of Four is not merely a location — it functions as a character. Doyle moves the action through starkly different parts of the city to reflect the themes of class, empire and moral confusion. Baker Street represents domestic order and Holmes’s intellectual world. The foggy journey to Pondicherry Lodge creates pathetic fallacy — the characters literally cannot see the truth. Thaddeus Sholto’s over-decorated room exposes gaudy colonial wealth. The Thames docks reveal industrial poverty. Each setting carries meaning.

The fog is Doyle’s most powerful recurring image. Watson describes a “dense drizzly fog” as they travel and notes that “the dull, heavy evening” creates a mood of uncertainty. In Victorian London, fog was real — caused by coal pollution from thousands of factories and homes — but Doyle uses it symbolically. Fog obscures, distorts and confuses. It represents the appearance versus reality theme: nothing in the novel is what it first seems.

Key Fact

Baker Street = order and intellect. The foggy streets = uncertainty and hidden truth. Thaddeus Sholto’s room = colonial excess. Pondicherry Lodge = Gothic horror and death. The Thames = the working-class underworld and the novel’s climactic violence. Doyle uses each location to reflect a different aspect of Victorian society.

The River Thames: Empire and Industry

The Thames is central to the novel’s climax. The river was Victorian London’s commercial artery — carrying trade goods from across the empire. During the chase, Watson describes “the dull blur of the lights” along the dockside, timber yards, and the “dense swarm” of boats. The Thames represents both Britain’s imperial power (the wealth flowing in) and its darker side (poverty, crime, pollution). It is fitting that the Agra treasure ends up in the river — swallowed by the same waterway that connects London to the empire from which it was stolen.

The Sign of Four uses a dual narrative structure. For most of the novel, Watson narrates events in the present tense as they unfold in London. Then, in Chapters 11–12, the narrative shifts to Jonathan Small’s first-person confession, which takes us back decades to India during the Rebellion of 1857. This structural shift is significant: it moves the reader from England to India, from the present to the past, and from the detective’s perspective to the criminal’s.

Small’s confession reframes everything the reader has seen. The ‘mystery’ becomes a story of imperial injustice, betrayal and revenge. Doyle’s decision to give Small his own narrative voice humanises him and complicates the moral structure. The embedded narrative technique forces the reader to reconsider who is truly the villain: Small, Sholto, or the empire that set events in motion.

Clues, Red Herrings and Reader Engagement

Detective fiction depends on the careful planting of clues and red herrings. Doyle is a master of both. The creosote on the rope is a genuine clue that leads Holmes to the killers. The small footprint tells Holmes about Tonga. The card reading “The sign of the four” connects the murder to the original pact. These clues are available to the reader, but their significance only becomes clear through Holmes’s deductions.

Toby the dog’s false trail to the creosote barrel is a red herring — it leads the investigation temporarily astray. Athelney Jones’s arrest of Thaddeus is another: Jones treats circumstantial evidence as proof, distracting from the real criminals. These false leads serve a structural purpose: they delay the resolution, increase tension, and demonstrate that detection requires patience and rigour, not hasty conclusions.

Key Fact

Genuine clues: creosote on the rope, the small footprint, the wooden-leg marks, the “sign of the four” card, the poison dart. Red herrings: Toby following the wrong creosote trail, Jones’s arrest of Thaddeus. Doyle gives the reader access to the same clues as Holmes, making the mystery feel fair even though Holmes solves it first.

The Science of Deduction

Holmes’s deductive method is the novel’s intellectual engine. He applies deductive reasoning at every stage: reading Watson’s watch, analysing the crime scene, identifying Tonga from a gazetteer, tracing the creosote. His approach mirrors the scientific method: observe, hypothesise, test, conclude. This reflects the Victorian reverence for science and rational thought.

Doyle’s pacing is deliberate. The novel begins slowly (domestic scene, watch deduction), then builds through mystery (Mary’s arrival), revelation (Thaddeus’s backstory), shock (Bartholomew’s murder), investigation (Holmes at the crime scene, Toby, the Irregulars), climax (Thames chase), and resolution (Small’s confession, Watson’s proposal). This arc follows the classic detective fiction structure but Doyle adds the dual narrative of Small’s confession, which shifts the genre from pure mystery to something more like a historical adventure.

The denouement is split: the detective plot resolves with Small’s capture, the romantic plot resolves with Watson’s proposal, and the character study resolves — or fails to resolve — with Holmes’s return to cocaine. This triple ending gives the examiner multiple angles to test.

For the exam, setting, structure and the science of deduction are all methods (AO2). When you write about fog, you are writing about Doyle’s use of pathetic fallacy. When you write about Small’s confession, you are writing about narrative structure. When you write about Holmes’s deductions, you are writing about how Doyle presents Victorian scientific ideals through character. Always name the technique and explain its effect.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Setting, structure and detection method are all assessable under AO2 (writer’s methods). When writing about setting, always link it to a theme: ‘Doyle uses the fog as pathetic fallacy to reflect the moral uncertainty of the case.’ When writing about structure, explain its effect: ‘The dual narrative forces the reader to reassess who the true villain is.’ Naming the technique and explaining its impact is what separates a Level 4 answer from a Level 2.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • London functions as a character: fog represents moral confusion, the Thames connects empire to crime, and contrasting locations reflect class divisions.
  • The dual narrative structure (Watson’s present / Small’s past) shifts the reader’s sympathy and complicates simple moral judgments about hero and villain.
  • Doyle plants genuine clues (creosote, footprints, the card) alongside red herrings (Toby’s false trail, Jones’s wrongful arrest) to make the mystery fair but suspenseful.

lessons.title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
lessons.description: Empire, justice, wealth, science and love explored, plus AQA extract-and-essay exam technique.
lessons.content_html:
Theme 1: Empire and Colonialism

The British Empire is not just a backdrop to The Sign of Four — it drives the entire plot. The colonial origins of the Agra treasure connect every crime in the novel to India. The treasure was stolen from a merchant during the Indian Rebellion of 1857. Major Sholto and Captain Morstan — British officers in India — became entangled in its story. Jonathan Small lost his leg serving the empire. Tonga was brought from the colonised Andaman Islands. The wealth that Victorians celebrated as a product of empire is shown by Doyle to be built on theft, violence and exploitation.

Watson himself embodies the empire’s human cost. He is a wounded veteran of the Second Anglo-Afghan War, injured at the Battle of Maiwand. Yet Watson does not question the empire — he is proud of his service. This tension is important for contextual analysis: Doyle does not explicitly criticise the empire, but the plot he constructs shows its destructive consequences. Examiners reward students who can identify this implicit critique rather than simply stating “the novel is about the empire.”

Key Fact

Doyle does not overtly condemn the British Empire, but the plot demonstrates its destructive consequences. Colonial violence in India creates crime in London. Watson is a proud imperial veteran, yet the treasure that drives the plot is stolen colonial wealth. Examiners reward students who identify this implicit critique through close analysis of Doyle’s choices.

Theme 2: Justice and Revenge

Who is truly guilty in The Sign of Four? The question is more complex than it first appears. Small murdered the merchant and orchestrated Bartholomew’s death. But Sholto betrayed Small and stole the treasure. The original merchant was carrying wealth extracted from colonial India. Doyle complicates the idea of justice by showing that every act of theft and violence flows from an earlier injustice.

Holmes restores a kind of order: Small is captured, the mystery is solved. But the treasure is lost, Tonga is dead without mourning, and the underlying injustice of empire remains untouched. Doyle suggests that the justice system can solve individual crimes but cannot address the systemic injustice that created them. This is sophisticated territory for an exam essay: you can argue that Doyle both supports and questions the idea of justice.

The Agra treasure is the novel’s central symbol of greed. Everyone who pursues it suffers. The merchant is murdered. The four conspirators are imprisoned for decades. Sholto steals it and dies tormented by guilt. Morstan dies in an argument about it. Bartholomew is murdered for it. Small throws it into the Thames rather than let anyone else have it.

Doyle’s moral is clear: stolen wealth brings only destruction. Yet there is an irony — the treasure’s loss is what makes Watson’s happiness possible. If Mary had inherited the treasure, Watson would have felt unable to propose because of the class difference. The elimination of wealth enables love. Doyle suggests that emotional wealth (love, friendship) is more valuable than material wealth.

Theme 4: Science and Reason

Holmes embodies the Victorian faith in reason. His deductive method is essentially the scientific method applied to crime: observe, hypothesise, test, conclude. His superiority over Athelney Jones demonstrates that evidence-based reasoning is more effective than assumption. Doyle, a trained doctor, champions this worldview through his hero.

However, Doyle also shows the limits of pure reason. Holmes cannot sustain human relationships. He dismisses Watson’s emotions with the cocaine syringe. His brilliance brings no personal fulfilment — only temporary relief from boredom. The cyclical structure (cocaine to cocaine) suggests that reason alone cannot create a meaningful life. Watson, with his warmth and capacity for love, achieves something Holmes cannot.

Key Fact

Doyle simultaneously champions reason (Holmes’s method solves the crime) and critiques its limitations (Holmes cannot achieve personal fulfilment). Science and deduction triumph professionally but fail personally. Watson, who combines intellect with emotion, achieves the happier ending. This duality is rich exam material.

Theme 5: Love and Relationships

The romance between Watson and Mary Morstan runs parallel to the detective plot. Watson is attracted to Mary from the moment she arrives, but class anxiety holds him back — if the treasure is found, she would be wealthy and ‘above’ him. When the treasure is lost, Watson is relieved: “the treasure is lost and the case is closed,” but he gains something more valuable. Doyle uses the romance to argue that human connection matters more than material wealth.

Holmes, by contrast, is entirely indifferent to love. When Watson announces his engagement, Holmes reaches for the cocaine. This juxtaposition at the novel’s close is structurally deliberate: Doyle places the two outcomes side by side to highlight what each character values and what each character lacks.

A typical nineteenth-century novel question gives you a printed extract of roughly 400 words and asks you to write about both the extract AND the novel as a whole. Your response needs a clear argument, close analysis of methods and embedded context. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact mark weightings that apply to you.

Step 1: Read the extract carefully. Underline key words, phrases, and techniques. Identify what the extract is about (character? theme? setting?).

Step 2: Plan your response. Aim for 3–4 paragraphs. Each paragraph should include: a point about Doyle’s presentation, a quotation (from the extract or the wider novel), analysis of language or structure, and a contextual link.

Step 3: Write about the extract first. Give close analysis of specific words and phrases. Then extend to the novel as a whole — link the extract’s themes to other moments in the text.

Step 4: Embed context. Do not write a separate context paragraph. Instead, weave it into your analysis: “Doyle’s use of dehumanising language for Tonga reflects the racial prejudice that underpinned Victorian imperial culture.”

Timing: Spend about 45–50 minutes on this question. Allow 5 minutes for planning and 5 for checking.

Key Quotations to Learn

Most nineteenth-century novel exams are closed book, but the extract is printed for you. For the ‘novel as a whole’ part of your response, you need to refer to events, characters and ideas from other parts of the text. Memorising a few key quotations will strengthen your response significantly, even though precise wording is not required.

“My mind rebels at stagnation” — Holmes on why he uses cocaine (character: restlessness, intellect without purpose).

“When you have eliminated the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth” — Holmes’s deductive principle (theme: science and reason).

“A seven-per-cent solution” — the cocaine injection (character: self-destruction, cyclical structure).

“The sign of the four” — the card at the murder scene (plot: connecting all crimes to the original pact).

“An unhallowed dwarf with his hideous face” — description of Tonga (context: racial prejudice, empire).

“It is a capital mistake to theorise before you have all the evidence” — Holmes warning against assumption (theme: science vs prejudice).

lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The five central themes — empire, justice, wealth, science and love — are all interconnected: the Agra treasure links colonial greed to personal destruction, and only when the treasure is lost can love flourish.
  • Doyle both champions and critiques Victorian ideals: science solves crimes but cannot bring fulfilment; the empire creates wealth but also violence; justice is achieved for individuals but not for systems.
  • In the AQA exam, analyse the extract closely first (specific words, phrases, techniques), then extend to the novel as a whole, embedding context in every paragraph.

practice_questions.text: Read the passage where Holmes reads from the gazetteer about the Andaman Islanders: ‘They are naturally hideous, having large, misshapen heads, small fierce eyes.’ How does Doyle use this moment to present ideas about empire and race?
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis. E.g. The gazetteer presents racist stereotypes as scientific fact, reflecting Victorian ‘scientific racism.’ ‘Naturally hideous’ normalises prejudice by making it seem biological. Holmes reads this without questioning it, showing how embedded these attitudes were. The gazetteer is a product of colonial knowledge production — categorising colonised peoples as inferior. Context: Victorian racial hierarchy, the Andaman Islands as a colonised territory.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification.

practice_questions.text: How does Doyle present the theme of justice in The Sign of Four? Write about the extract and the novel as a whole.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Sophisticated analysis. Justice is complicated: Small is captured but was himself betrayed; the treasure was stolen multiple times; Tonga is killed without trial; the underlying injustice of empire remains. Holmes restores individual order but cannot address systemic problems. Small’s confession complicates moral judgment. The lost treasure means no one benefits from the original crime. Doyle questions whether true justice is achievable.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Doyle explore the theme of wealth and greed in The Sign of Four? Write about the extract and the novel as a whole.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Sophisticated analysis. The Agra treasure destroys everyone who pursues it: murder, betrayal, imprisonment, death. Small throws it into the Thames out of spite. Yet its loss enables Watson’s happiness — removing the class barrier to his proposal. Thaddeus sends pearls from guilt, showing wealth cannot ease conscience. Doyle’s moral: material wealth corrupts; emotional wealth (love, friendship) endures. The treasure’s colonial origins connect personal greed to imperial exploitation.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Doyle use the contrast between Holmes and Watson to explore the limits of science and reason? You should refer to the whole text in your response.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (11-12) Convincing, critical analysis. Holmes = reason, science, deduction; Watson = emotion, warmth, love. Holmes solves the crime but returns to cocaine; Watson finds personal fulfilment through marriage. The cyclical structure suggests reason alone is insufficient. Doyle champions the scientific method (Holmes is superior to Jones) but shows its personal cost. Watson’s narration mediates between intellect and emotion. Context: Victorian reverence for science and the Romantic tradition of the tortured genius.
Upper band (9-10) Thoughtful analysis.
Top band (7-8): Clear understanding.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Some understanding.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Limited response.
Lower band (1-2): Simple statements.

practice_questions.text: How does the romantic subplot between Watson and Mary Morstan reflect Victorian attitudes to class and gender?
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis. E.g. Watson feels he cannot propose to a wealthy Mary — Victorian men were expected to be the financial provider. The lost treasure removes this class barrier, suggesting Doyle sees class rules as obstacles to genuine love. Mary is defined through the romance: her story ends with a proposal rather than independence. Watson describes her through a romantic male gaze. Context: Victorian courtship conventions, the governess as ambiguous class position.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification.
